{"id": "12:33/q15", "question": "What does aṣbu ilayhinna mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣabā conveys inclination, practical compliance, or the more intense ṣabābah.", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q15/p1", "position": "I incline toward, long for, or turn toward the women through desire.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and al-Ṭabarī cite poetry about a heart inclining toward Hind; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Māwardī repeat it. Al-Zajjāj connects ṣabā to amusement; al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī connect ṣabā to the pleasant east wind. Al-Rāghib adds yearning and childlike action; al-Majmaʿ describes softness of passion. Asad combines inclination, yearning and amorous indulgence. Abū Ḥayyān stresses inclination alone does not entail the forbidden act."}, {"id": "12:33/q15/p2", "position": "I follow, comply with, or yield to the women.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās gloss the consequence as following or complying; al-Māwardī includes both compliance and inclination."}, {"id": "12:33/q15/p3", "position": "I yearn intensely, as passion pours toward its object.", "reasons": "The minority derivation is from ṣabābah; al-Samīn likens it to water poured toward what is loved."}]}
{"id": "12:33/q16", "question": "How is aṣbu read and derived?", "turns_on": "The consonant doubling and derivation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q16/p1", "position": "The common reading has a light b and derives from ṣabā yaṣbū.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān connect it with ṣabwah, desire or play."}, {"id": "12:33/q16/p2", "position": "A group doubles b, deriving the word from ṣabābah, intense yearning.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn explains the image as love poured like water; al-Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī mention the variant."}]}
{"id": "12:33/q17", "question": "What does 'among the ignorant' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ignorance is sinful conduct, unused knowledge, or foolishness.", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q17/p1", "position": "Those who sin and disregard God's rights, limits and commands.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Isḥāq identify disobedience; Ibn ʿAbbās says sinners and offenders; al-Baghawī and ʿAmr b. Murra say even knowing sinners are ignorant during the act. Bursevī calls adulterers lying ignoramuses."}, {"id": "12:33/q17/p2", "position": "Those who possess knowledge but fail to act on it.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says they become like the ignorant; al-Nasafī and Ālūsī repeat the contrast. Bursevī says such knowledge has no practical value; Abū Ḥayyān calls it unbeneficial knowledge."}, {"id": "12:33/q17/p3", "position": "Foolish or unwise people, deserving blame for irrational misconduct.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī's people of meanings say 'deserving blame'; al-Ṭabrisī allows 'acting as though ignorant.' Al-Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī and Ālūsī say a wise person would not do this; a poetic line uses ignorance for folly. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds lack of forbearance."}]}
{"id": "12:33/q18", "question": "Why say 'one of the ignorant' instead of simply 'ignorant'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q18/p1", "position": "Joining their class is stronger than merely bearing the quality.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 'one of the disgraced' at 12:32."}]}
{"id": "12:33/q19", "question": "Was Joseph asking to be imprisoned, and how was his prayer answered?", "turns_on": "Whether the first clause constitutes a request for prison or prepares the actual request for protection.", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q19/p1", "position": "The declaration is a prayer or choice for imprisonment, and he was tested with what he asked for.", "reasons": "A report says God told him he confined himself; Ibn ʿUyayna's ant and rock report says prayer accords with decree and Joseph should have trusted God's care. {"id": "12:33/q20", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from Joseph's choice and dependence?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward focus is the heart's vulnerability, prison's spiritual use, or love that overcomes temptation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q20/p1", "position": "The heart needs continual divine protection from the soul's enduring attraction.", "reasons": "Qāshānī describes the heart's two faces toward spirit and soul; temporary illumination cannot secure it. {"id": "12:33/q21", "question": "What grammatical analogies for feminine and proper-name plurals appear with the verse's feminine plural?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q21/p1", "position": "Arabic pluralizes names by sound or attested broken patterns, with form and established usage controlling the choice.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives Zayd, ʿAmr, Bakr, Qays, Saʿd, Kaʿb and other names; women may take -āt or broken plurals, with dialectal heavy and light tāʾ. Names with tāʾ marbūṭa avoid masculine -ūn; Warqāʾ follows adjective patterns. He surveys Ibn, Ism, Imruʾ, Umm, Shāh, Ḍarb, Rubba, Ẓuba, ʿIdda, Shafa, Ama, Burda, faʿīl/faʿīla names, participles and ʿAjūz, preserving attested forms. Jarīr, Ruʾba, al-Farazdaq, Laqīṭ and others supply poetic witnesses; Yūnus and al-Khalīl attest frequency. He rejects unestablished forms such as ḥumr for Aḥmar and shafāt/umāt, and uses diminutives to support ʿUthmānūn rather than ʿathāmīn."}]}
{"id": "12:33/q22", "question": "What can waw do before a verb in a nonaffirmative construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q22/p1", "position": "It may introduce a subjunctive verb with an implied an, coordinate, or begin an independent raised verb, with different meanings.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says subjunctive waw can prohibit or require the combination of two acts, unlike jussive separation; waw alone does not assert sequence as fa does. His examples include al-Akhṭal, al-Ḥuṭayʾa, Durayd, al-Aʿshā, Kaʿb al-Ghanawī and Qays b. Zuhayr. 'Visit me and I visit you' distinguishes a committed raised clause from joint prospective action; noun plus verb under aḥabb requires implied an. Some examples admit raised attachment to a noun or relative clause."}]}
{"id": "12:33/q23", "question": "What wider principles of Qur'an recitation and pause are recorded alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "The aims of recitation, pause criteria, and rival explanations or strength of the completion report.", "positions": [{"id": "12:33/q23/p1", "position": "Measured recitation with reflection is preferable to speed and volume.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr prefers understanding and practice; Mujāhid values the reader of less text with equal prayer movements. Early Muslims repeated one verse until dawn; al-Ghazālī says deliberate reading moves even a non-Arabic reader's heart. {"id": "12:91/q01", "question": "What does the oath تالله express?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q01/p1", "position": "The brothers swear by God in a form that venerates Him; the oath tāʾ is restricted to Allah’s name.", "reasons": "Al-Samarraʾi counts five Qurʾanic uses, three in Joseph (12:73, 12:85, 12:91) and two in al-Naḥl (16:56, 16:63). {"id": "12:91/q03", "question": "What does آثرك mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q03/p1", "position": "It means God chose or preferred Joseph over others, favoring him with gifts and special standing.", "reasons": "Muqatil compares the choosing in 20:72. {"id": "12:91/q10", "question": "What does the brothers’ confession accomplish?", "turns_on": "The sources emphasize different effects of the same admission: an appeal to Joseph and a reversal of the brothers’ earlier judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q10/p1", "position": "It apologizes, admits guilt, and indirectly asks Joseph for pardon or kindness.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi places the apology after Joseph identifies himself in 12:90. {"id": "12:91/q12", "question": "How is وإن كنا لخاطئين constructed and emphasized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q12/p1", "position": "The conjunction gives their state; إن is lightened, خاطئين is kāna’s accusative predicate, and the lām reinforces the assertion.", "reasons": "Jishumi identifies the accusative predicate. {"id": "12:91/q17", "question": "What happens when the brothers recognize Joseph?", "turns_on": "The reports supply different details of the recognition scene.", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q17/p1", "position": "They apologize after he identifies himself and recognize his forbearance.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi connects the apology to Joseph’s identification in 12:90. {"id": "12:91/q18", "question": "How does Joseph respond to his brothers’ wrongdoing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q18/p1", "position": "He forgives them without exposing or rebuking them; ‘no reproach’ is praised as beautiful forgiveness.", "reasons": "Qatada says he did not expose or rebuke them. {"id": "12:91/q19", "question": "How does their wording to Joseph differ from their request to Jacob?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q19/p1", "position": "To Joseph they imply guilt without naming the offense or explicitly requesting forgiveness; to Jacob they request forgiveness and confess sins with emphatic إنّا.", "reasons": "Al-Samarraʾi compares the light in here with their address to Jacob in 12:98."}]}
{"id": "12:91/q20", "question": "What does the brothers’ outcome teach about God’s direction of human affairs?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different lessons from the same reversal: irresistible divine gift, patient trust, hidden providence, and the consequences of wrongdoing.", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q20/p1", "position": "Envy cannot prevent a blessing God decrees.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu cites the Prophet’s prayer that none can withhold what God grants or grant what He withholds. It also cites Ziya Pasha’s couplet in which divine power makes tyrants finally admit God’s preference for another."}, {"id": "12:91/q20/p2", "position": "The story teaches patience, measured action, and trust as difficult events unfold gradually under divine wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi links this to 12:110 and says ordered causes test both obedience and disobedience."}, {"id": "12:91/q20/p3", "position": "God directs human affairs beyond people’s grasp; what they hate may benefit them and what they love may harm them.", "reasons": "Asad contrasts the Qurʾanic story with Genesis’ romantic account and cites 2:216."}, {"id": "12:91/q20/p4", "position": "Worldly outcomes reveal consequences of wrongdoing: Joseph receives kingship while his brothers stand before him as humbled petitioners.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi contrasts Joseph’s kingship with their abasement."}]}
{"id": "12:91/q21", "question": "How was Joseph’s forgiveness later echoed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:91/q21/p1", "position": "At the conquest of Mecca, Muhammad cited Joseph’s forgiveness and freed Quraysh after they acknowledged his noble standing.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports the Prophet’s action and calls Joseph’s no-reproach response a beautiful form of forgiveness."}]}

{"id": "12:92/q02", "question": "What does Joseph promise with لا تثريب عليكم?", "turns_on": "The notes variously take the negation as ending censure, preserving the relationship, removing concrete penalty, or denying aversion.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q02/p1", "position": "He pardons his brothers and will not blame, rebuke, taunt, publicize or recall their offense.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq locate the wrong against Joseph himself; al-Suddi and al-Kalbi stress that he will not mention it again. Qatadah says he neither broadcast nor reproached it. Al-Tha'labi calls his answer forbearing and guided; Ibn Atiyya calls it gracious, reporting Ikrima that God raised Joseph's renown for it. Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih make the promise permanent; al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi say it begins after that day. The brothers' confession precedes his pardon in al-Razi, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Jishumi; al-Tabataba'i stresses that they stood powerless. The Study Quran calls this a beautiful form of forgiveness."}, {"id": "12:92/q02/p2", "position": "He will not alter or damage their brotherly bond and rights.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari explicitly names the rights of brotherhood and cites Sufyan for no change; al-Mawardi transmits Sufyan ibn Uyayna's no alteration gloss. Al-Qurtubi reports al-Zajjaj's kinship and pardon reading."}, {"id": "12:92/q02/p3", "position": "He will inflict no punishment or harm on them.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi lists no punishment; al-Jishumi says no injury that spoils their condition; the Study Quran observes that reproach can include physical punishment. Al-Qushayri says their shame already sufficed as punishment."}, {"id": "12:92/q02/p4", "position": "He will neither investigate their deed nor rebuke them over it.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi attributes this gloss to Sufyan and Abu Ali."}, {"id": "12:92/q02/p5", "position": "He bears no aversion or objection toward them.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi reports Mujahid's gloss as no aversion to what they said; al-Durr reports Mujahid as no resistance or objection."}]}
{"id": "12:92/q03", "question": "How is لا تثريب عليكم constructed grammatically?", "turns_on": "The parses differ over the omitted predicate, whether عليكم is its expression or an adjective, and what kind of generality the negative form conveys.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q03/p1", "position": "لا negates the entire genus, with indefinite تثريب built on fatḥa and an understood predicate; عليكم expresses the predicate or its relation.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi calls تثريب an indefinite singular noun built with lā; al-Zarkashi says lā can operate like inna and often omits a known predicate, citing 33:13, 16:62, 11:47 and 2:254. Al-Farisi and al-Samin bar direct government of the following complements by a built verbal noun. Ibn Ashur compares the self-contained idiom لا بأس and Q 75:11."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p2", "position": "عليكم is an adjective to تثريب, while اليوم is the temporal predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi allows an implied modifier; al-Hawfi gives this parse and Abu Hayyan calls it good; al-Samin states it directly. Al-Farisi also allows اليوم to modify the adjective of عليكم with an omitted predicate."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p3", "position": "عليكم is the predicate, with اليوم attached to it or to its implied stability.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi gives a parse with no separate adjective and also an omitted-predicate variant. Al-Samin says عليكم is the predicate; al-Radi says اليوم is governed by it, while the reverse is possible. Al-Alusi links عليكم to an omitted predicate and allows اليوم on that predicate or its adverbial phrase."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p4", "position": "An omitted verb supplies 'no reproach will reproach you today.'", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls this strong because Arabic often omits a known predicate after lā. Al-Samin reports the parallel to لا عاصم اليوم من أمر الله (11:43), but objects that this verse would require two omissions and a metaphorical verb, where the parallel needs one omission and a literal verb."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p5", "position": "عليكم is an explanatory complement like لك in سقيا لك, or it and اليوم attach to an implied verb.", "reasons": "Al-Samin records both alternatives, the latter with lā's predicate omitted and a verb supplied from تثريب."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p6", "position": "لا تثريب is accusative as a verbal noun; اليوم may be accusative under negation or nominative under an implied ليس بتثريب.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi gives both case analyses."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p7", "position": "A non-governing لا can also negate the whole genus, though its built governing form signals generality more strongly.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi rejects al-Zamakhshari and al-Hariri's restriction to one instance; Ibn al-Hajib invokes the grammarians' agreement that indefinites in negation generalize."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p8", "position": "A non-governing لا denies only one instance, rather than the entire genus.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Hariri are reported with this restriction; al-Zarkashi and Ibn al-Hajib object that indefinite negation can be general."}, {"id": "12:92/q03/p9", "position": "اليوم is the predicate of لا, while عليكم attaches to the predication implicit in that adverb.", "reasons": "Al-Samin presents this as another construction."}]}
{"id": "12:92/q04", "question": "How does اليوم attach, and why specify today?", "turns_on": "The pause after عليكم or اليوم, the scope of today, and whether a built verbal noun may govern a separated adverb decide the readings.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q04/p1", "position": "It qualifies no reproach at the very moment blame or revenge would be expected, assuring no later reproach either.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari calls it the first moment of pardon; al-Jishumi calls it the first revelation of Joseph's identity, when revenge was possible, or the end of earlier rebuke. Al-Wahidi says confession ended his previous reproach. Al-Razi argues that denying the whole kind of reproach now excludes every instance in every circumstance; al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Biqa'i and al-Alusi infer still less blame later. Al-Tabataba'i adds that the brothers were powerless. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin attach today to an omitted stability predicate, and most readers pause after today."}, {"id": "12:92/q04/p2", "position": "Today means the present period, or the whole future span of his pardon.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites Imru' al-Qays, and al-Tabrisi and al-Murtada cite poetic lines, to show that اليوم can mean an extended time. Ibn Ashur compares 5:3. Al-Jishumi also reports the whole-span interpretation."}, {"id": "12:92/q04/p3", "position": "It begins the forgiveness clause: 'Today God forgives you,' as prayer, glad tidings, or declaration.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash permits a pause after عليكم; al-Tabrisi reports his preference and analogy to لا ريب فيه. Al-Wahidi calls this weaker because a following prayer ordinarily cannot govern a prior adverb, though the indicative permits it. Al-Samin says the pause explains the reading; Ibn Ashur finds the preceding idiom ends at عليكم and its addition intensifies reassurance. Al-Murtada's attachment is challenged on prayer syntax. The declaration reading draws objection from Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi because certainty requires revelation; al-Alusi considers responses under the forgiveness question."}, {"id": "12:92/q04/p4", "position": "It directly modifies the verbal noun تثريب.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari lists this among three attachments. Al-Farisi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, the Itqan and Abu al-Baqa object: a built indefinite verbal noun cannot have its complement separated by عليكم, and quasi-annexation would demand inflection or tanwin. Al-Alusi qualifies the tanwin argument with grammatical texts and an agreed hadith where quasi-annexed nouns lack tanwin; authorities dispute whether these are built. Al-Samin recounts al-Farisi's poetry on كفران and Ibn Malik's analysis of لا صمت يوم إلى الليل."}]}

{"id": "12:92/q06", "question": "What grounds or scope do the notes give for divine forgiveness here?", "turns_on": "The grounds named are the brothers' penitence and Joseph's waiver of his own claim; the notes also differ over how broadly the request extends.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q06/p1", "position": "Their repentance, confession, shame, regret and return to obedience invite God's forgiveness.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari puts Ibn Ishaq's prayer after admission and says God's mercy reaches those who repent and return. Al-Mawardi lists repentance, confession and regret; Ibn Abi Hatim's Ibn Ismail says Joseph promised forgiveness on acknowledgment. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi likewise join forgiveness to confession, and al-Islahi calls their regret sincere. Abu Hayyan notes that certainty on this ground can reflect a Mu'tazili premise that forgiveness requires repentance; Ibn Ashur places it under prior law."}, {"id": "12:92/q06/p2", "position": "Joseph's pardon of his own claim allows or entails God's forgiveness of them.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi reports that God forgives because Joseph made pardon permissible; al-Alusi reports an inference from Joseph's pardon and God's promise to accept repentance. Al-Bursevi distinguishes Joseph's waived personal claim from what God must forgive."}, {"id": "12:92/q06/p3", "position": "The request includes all who wronged Joseph, even brothers absent at this meeting.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i invokes a later statement at 12:95 for the absence of some brothers."}, {"id": "12:92/q06/p4", "position": "The prayer reaches their past offenses and possible future lapses.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i takes the imperfect as fostering sincere repentance and hope in the Most Merciful."}]}
{"id": "12:92/q07", "question": "Why call God أرحم الراحمين here?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing mercy formula points chiefly to the brothers' hoped-for forgiveness or Joseph's own elevation.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q07/p1", "position": "God's greater mercy gives hope that He will accept Joseph's prayer and forgive repentant sinners.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi also takes it as God's mercy in pardoning the brothers' earlier offense. Al-Tabari says God is most merciful to those who return to obedience; al-Wahidi reports Ibn Abbas that God is more merciful to devoted servants than parents to children. Abu Hayyan makes mercy the reason for Joseph's hope. Al-Nasafi contrasts Joseph's poor, miserly human mercy with the rich, forgiving God's; al-Baydawi says God forgives small and great sins. Al-Alusi says all created mercy comes from God, while God alone forgives every scale of sin and accepts penitents."}, {"id": "12:92/q07/p2", "position": "It recalls God's mercy in making Joseph a king.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives this as an alternative; al-Tabrisi likewise connects Joseph's pardon with God's elevation of him."}]}
{"id": "12:92/q08", "question": "How was Joseph's pardon applied at the conquest of Mecca?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q08/p1", "position": "The Prophet quoted Joseph's pardon to Quraysh after asking what they expected, and forgave or released them.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi places the exchange after two rak'ahs in the Kaaba and includes a prayer for forgiveness. {"id": "12:92/q09", "question": "What other proclamations accompany the conquest-day pardon report?", "turns_on": "These are distinct accompanying proclamations, rather than rival versions of one ruling.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q09/p1", "position": "The Prophet abolished pre-Islamic claims for usury, blood and property while preserving Kaaba custodianship and pilgrims' water service.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi transmits this in the same conquest account."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p2", "position": "He ended ancestral boasting, recalling descent from Adam and honor by piety.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi connects this proclamation to 49:13."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p3", "position": "He assigned aggravated blood payment of one hundred camels, forty pregnant, for a mistaken quasi-intentional killing with stick or whip.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi records this legal detail."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p4", "position": "He declared Mecca sacred from creation, with only a one-hour permission to him that day.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi reports that its sanctity held before and after him."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p5", "position": "He barred disturbing Mecca's game, cutting thorn trees or grass, and taking lost property except to announce it.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi lists these restrictions."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p6", "position": "He excepted idhkhir from the vegetation ban.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi says al-Abbas requested it for smiths and roofs; the Prophet paused before allowing it."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p7", "position": "A later herald forbade bequests to an heir.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi says the herald was sent after leaving Mecca."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p8", "position": "The herald assigned the child to the marital bed and the stone to the adulterer.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi transmits this proclamation."}, {"id": "12:92/q09/p9", "position": "The herald said a woman may not give away her property without her husband's permission.", "reasons": "Al-Azraqi transmits this additional proclamation."}]}

{"id": "12:92/q15", "question": "Why did Joseph forgive at once while Jacob deferred his prayer?", "turns_on": "The explanations invoke age, affection, differing harm and benefit, delayed readiness to pray, or how the sons addressed each father and brother.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q15/p1", "position": "Young Joseph was easier to ask, forgiving at once; older Jacob promised to ask later.", "reasons": "Ata al-Khurasani gives this contrast through Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Durr."}, {"id": "12:92/q15/p2", "position": "Jacob loved them more and first reproached them; Joseph forgave promptly on their confession.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri offers this contrast and notes the brothers' shame itself punished them."}, {"id": "12:92/q15/p3", "position": "Joseph saw benefit and blessing from their act, whereas Jacob had borne continuing grief and blindness.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi reports his shaykh that Joseph's gratitude led to immediate forgiveness while Jacob awaited sincere, divinely permitted intent. {"id": "12:92/q16", "question": "What moral example does Joseph's pardon set?", "turns_on": "The notes explain the example through noble pardon or awareness of divine decree.", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q16/p1", "position": "It is exceptional, generous forgiveness to emulate, especially when the forgiver has power and receives an apology.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports the sons of Imran al-Jawni had heard no pardon like it, and Malik ibn Dinar reports al-Hasan that Scripture preserves it as an example; al-Durr transmits Abu Imran's praise. {"id": "12:92/q17", "question": "What inward reading is given to the brothers' wrongdoing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:92/q17/p1", "position": "Their original wrong became a means of Joseph's elevation and kingship, prompting his prayer for them.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi transmits the Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya's inward reading."}]}
